analysis.one_liner: Requires automatic and same-day voter registration, paper ballots, and early and mail voting nationwide.
analysis.headline: John Lewis's bill to modernize voter registration and expand voting access sat in six House committees for nearly two years and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced by the late Rep. John Lewis, would force every state to make it dramatically easier to register and vote: automatic registration through government agencies, online and same-day registration, early voting, no-excuse voting by mail, paper ballots that can be recounted, and an Election Day holiday. It would restore federal voting rights to people who finished prison sentences, bar the state's top election official from running campaigns, and give states federal money to cover the changes. It was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced and none of them ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Eligible citizens who are not registered, hourly workers who cannot take time off on a single Election Day, voters with disabilities, military and overseas families, and people who completed prison sentences but lost their voting rights. Anyone who has been wrongly purged from the rolls gains protections too, since states could no longer remove voters simply for skipping elections or ignoring a notice.

how_it_helps.text: States must set up automatic voter registration that electronically transfers registration information from agencies — motor vehicle offices, Social Security, Medicaid, universities, and others — to election officials unless the person declines [S3].
States must allow online registration, same-day registration at the polling place, early voting, and voting by mail without added conditions [S2].
States must use paper ballots that voters can verify, with manual counting for recounts and audits, and get federal grants for poll worker recruitment and risk-limiting election audits [S2].

States may not remove a voter from the rolls based merely on failure to vote or failure to respond to a notice [S3], and a new federal crime punishes hindering or interfering with someone registering to vote [S3].

The bill restores the right to vote in federal elections to citizens who have completed a criminal sentence [S3], makes Election Day a federal holiday [S3], expands voting access for people with disabilities [S3], and permanently reauthorizes the Election Assistance Commission [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the bill's grants, including $500 million for states to build automatic registration systems plus money for poll workers and election audits [S3]. States bear the cost of rebuilding registration and voting systems to federal requirements, and election equipment vendors face a paper-ballot mandate that would force many jurisdictions to replace machines. Chief state election officials would be barred from campaigning for candidates [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state election rules wholesale: states would have to accept automatic registration fed from many agencies, same-day registration, and no-excuse mail voting regardless of how they currently run elections [S2, S3].

Automatic registration routes personal data — including citizenship information and partial Social Security numbers — from a long list of government agencies into state voter databases, and although the bill sets security standards and privacy limits [S3], critics of federal registration mandates have argued such systems expand the attack surface and raise privacy concerns.

It authorizes at least $500 million in federal grants for automatic registration, plus separate grants for poll workers and audits, a cost an honest supporter would have to defend against other uses [S3].

Requiring paper ballots and manual counting for recounts and audits would force many jurisdictions to replace voting equipment on a federal timetable, a transition that costs money and can strain local election offices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The access gains are large and broadly distributed: fewer voters turned away, purged, or unable to reach a polling place, plus a stronger paper trail for counting votes. The costs are real — several hundred million dollars in federal grants, compliance work in all 50 states, and a federal override of state election procedures — and privacy and security questions around agency data-sharing deserved debate. Weighing those costs against the scale of change, the bill is a substantial expansion of voting access whose costs fall mainly on governments and election vendors rather than on individual voters.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees the day it was introduced, got bounced to two subcommittees, and never came back out for a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis introduced the bill on February 14, 2019, joined at introduction by Reps. Jim Clyburn, Steny Hoyer, and Jerrold Nadler [S3].
It was referred that day to the House Administration Committee and five others — Judiciary, Science, Space and Technology, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, and Education and Labor [S5].
In February and March 2019 it was referred to two subcommittees, and no committee or subcommittee ever reported it; the bill received no vote in either chamber [S5].

The bill's core voter registration and voting access provisions overlapped heavily with H.R. 1, the broader 'For the People Act' that House Democrats made their first major bill of the Congress; that bill passed the House on a party-line vote in March 2019 but never received a vote in the Republican-controlled Senate [widely reported].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the Voter Empowerment Act still sitting in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No change occurred, so state election systems and the companies that supply them kept the status quo, and state officials kept their current control over registration and voting rules. Opponents of federal election mandates and of expanded voting access are better off because the bill never moved, while voters who would have gained easier registration got nothing. The bill's provisions had a partial afterlife in the parallel H.R. 1, which also failed to become law in that Congress [widely reported].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo election systems and officials

for.name: Rep. John Lewis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Voter Empowerment Act of 2019 on February 14, 2019.

for.name: Reps. Jim Clyburn, Steny Hoyer, and Jerrold Nadler
for.role: House Democratic Caucus Chair, Majority Leader, and Judiciary Chair
for.what_they_did: Joined as original co-introducers when the bill was filed.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction (six committees)
against.role: House Administration, Judiciary, Science/Space/Technology, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Reform, Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire Congress without holding a markup or reporting it out; no committee ever advanced it.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Spent the Congress's floor time on the broader H.R. 1 election and ethics package, which absorbed most of this bill's provisions, rather than bringing the Voter Empowerment Act to the floor.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a vote on the parallel election-overhaul package (H.R. 1) that passed the House, leaving election modernization without a path to law.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a House Democrat, and the comparable election-access package (H.R. 1) that reached a House floor vote passed almost entirely on Democratic votes, while the Senate Republican majority gave it no vote; no Republican cosponsored this bill [S4].

industries.note: A federal paper-ballot mandate would cut the market for paperless touchscreen machines, but the bill's grants for automatic registration systems, poll worker training, and election audits would channel substantial public money to vendors of registration software and election equipment. Voters would get a verifiable paper trail either way.

The bill bars commercial use of information collected through automatic registration and restricts disclosure of registration data [S3], shrinking commercially available data from new registrants, while leaving existing political uses of voter files untouched. The public interest runs toward keeping agency-collected personal data out of commerce.

industries.industry: Chief state election officials and state election administration
industries.note: State election offices would receive federal grant money but would lose discretion over registration and voting rules and would be barred from campaign activity by the state's top election official [S2, S3]. The public gains uniform national access rules; the officials lose control.
